passages.title: Sleep Study on Modern-Day Hunter-Gatherers Dispels Popular Notions

headerUnits.sourceNormalizedText: Sleep Study on Modern-Day Hunter-Gatherers Dispels Popular Notions
headerUnits.translationNormalizedText: 现代狩猎采集者睡眠研究打破流行观念

source.text: Sleep Study on Modern-Day Hunter-Gatherers Dispels Popular Notions

translation.text: 现代狩猎采集者睡眠研究打破流行观念

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The sleep troubles common in modern life have long been blamed on our industrial society, from the city lights, long work hours and commutes, to caffeine and the Internet. Sleep researchers often look back on a time when humans were able to get more rest by sleeping and waking to the rhythms of the sun. It turns out that this may not be quite right. In fact, our ancestors may not have been getting the recommended eight hours of sleep, either.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 现代生活中常见的睡眠问题，长期以来一直被归咎于工业社会：从城市灯光、漫长工时和通勤，到咖啡因和互联网，种种因素都在其中。睡眠研究人员常常回顾一个过去的时代，认为当时人类可以随着太阳的节律入睡和醒来，获得更多休息。事实证明，这种看法可能并不完全正确。实际上，我们的祖先或许也没有达到建议的8小时睡眠。

source.text: The sleep troubles common in modern life have long been blamed on our industrial society, from the city lights, long work hours and commutes, to caffeine and the Internet.

translation.text: 现代生活中常见的睡眠问题，长期以来一直被归咎于工业社会：从城市灯光、漫长工时和通勤，到咖啡因和互联网，种种因素都在其中。

source.text: Sleep researchers often look back on a time when humans were able to get more rest by sleeping and waking to the rhythms of the sun.

translation.text: 睡眠研究人员常常回顾一个过去的时代，认为当时人类可以随着太阳的节律入睡和醒来，获得更多休息。

source.text: It turns out that this may not be quite right.

translation.text: 事实证明，这种看法可能并不完全正确。

source.text: In fact, our ancestors may not have been getting the recommended eight hours of sleep, either.

translation.text: 实际上，我们的祖先或许也没有达到建议的8小时睡眠。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: In a recent study, researchers traveled all over the world to examine sleep in some of the world’s last remaining hunter-gatherer societies – the Hadza of Tanzania, the San of Namibia, and the Tsimane of Bolivia. Cut off from media, electricity and other distractions, these pre-industrial societies are thought to sleep the way humans did more than 10,000 years ago. Traveling to where they lived, often in humid, remote locations, researchers used medical devices to record the sleeping habits of 94 of these tribespeople and ended up collecting data representing 1,165 days.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 在近期一项研究中，研究人员奔赴世界各地，调查一些世界上仅存的狩猎采集社会的睡眠情况，包括坦桑尼亚的哈扎人、纳米比亚的桑人和玻利维亚的齐马内人。这些前工业社会与媒体、电力和其他干扰隔绝，人们认为他们的睡眠方式与1万多年前的人类相同。研究人员前往他们的居住地——通常是潮湿偏远的地区——使用医疗设备记录94名部落成员的睡眠习惯，最终收集到相当于1,165天的数据。

source.text: In a recent study, researchers traveled all over the world to examine sleep in some of the world’s last remaining hunter-gatherer societies – the Hadza of Tanzania, the San of Namibia, and the Tsimane of Bolivia.

translation.text: 在近期一项研究中，研究人员奔赴世界各地，调查一些世界上仅存的狩猎采集社会的睡眠情况，包括坦桑尼亚的哈扎人、纳米比亚的桑人和玻利维亚的齐马内人。

source.text: Cut off from media, electricity and other distractions, these pre-industrial societies are thought to sleep the way humans did more than 10,000 years ago.

translation.text: 这些前工业社会与媒体、电力和其他干扰隔绝，人们认为他们的睡眠方式与1万多年前的人类相同。

source.text: Traveling to where they lived, often in humid, remote locations, researchers used medical devices to record the sleeping habits of 94 of these tribespeople and ended up collecting data representing 1,165 days.

translation.text: 研究人员前往他们的居住地——通常是潮湿偏远的地区——使用医疗设备记录94名部落成员的睡眠习惯，最终收集到相当于1,165天的数据。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: They found very similar sleep patterns despite their geographic isolation. On average, all three groups sleep a little less than 6.5 hours a night, do not take naps, and don’t go to sleep when it gets dark. Like many of us, the Hadza, San, and Tsimane spend more time in bed – from 6.9 to 8.5 hours – than they do actually sleeping. This adds up to a sleep efficiency that is very similar to today’s industrial populations.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 研究人员发现，尽管三个群体在地理上彼此隔绝，他们的睡眠模式却非常相似。三个群体每晚平均都睡不到6.5小时，不午睡，也不会天一黑就入睡。与我们许多人一样，哈扎人、桑人和齐马内人躺在床上的时间为6.9至8.5小时，比实际睡眠时间更长。由此计算出的睡眠效率，与今天工业社会人群的睡眠效率十分相近。

source.text: They found very similar sleep patterns despite their geographic isolation.

translation.text: 研究人员发现，尽管三个群体在地理上彼此隔绝，他们的睡眠模式却非常相似。

source.text: On average, all three groups sleep a little less than 6.5 hours a night, do not take naps, and don’t go to sleep when it gets dark.

translation.text: 三个群体每晚平均都睡不到6.5小时，不午睡，也不会天一黑就入睡。

source.text: Like many of us, the Hadza, San, and Tsimane spend more time in bed – from 6.9 to 8.5 hours – than they do actually sleeping.

translation.text: 与我们许多人一样，哈扎人、桑人和齐马内人躺在床上的时间为6.9至8.5小时，比实际睡眠时间更长。

source.text: This adds up to a sleep efficiency that is very similar to today’s industrial populations.

translation.text: 由此计算出的睡眠效率，与今天工业社会人群的睡眠效率十分相近。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: According to Jerome Siegel, director of the University of California’s Center for Sleep Research, evidence suggests sleep habits may not be environmental or cultural, but central to the physical makeup of humans. These findings question the millions of dollars that have been spent on research that tries to explain why some sleepers get only about six hours of sleep a night. Also, such findings question whether lack of sleep is a cause of obesity, mood disorders, and other physical and mental illnesses which have become so common in recent decades. Scientists have documented that people’s energy often falls in the mid-afternoon. Some have suggested that it’s because we’ve managed to suppress a natural desire for a nap.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 加州大学睡眠研究中心主任 Jerome Siegel 表示，证据显示，睡眠习惯可能并非由环境或文化决定，而是人类生理构造的核心特征。这些发现令人质疑：为解释一些睡眠者为何每晚只睡约6小时而投入的数百万美元研究，是否建立在正确前提上。它们也让人怀疑，近几十年来日益常见的肥胖、情绪障碍以及其他身心疾病，是否真由睡眠不足引起。科学家已经记录到，人们的精力往往会在下午中段下降。有人认为，这是因为我们设法压制了自然产生的午睡欲望。

source.text: According to Jerome Siegel, director of the University of California’s Center for Sleep Research, evidence suggests sleep habits may not be environmental or cultural, but central to the physical makeup of humans.

translation.text: 加州大学睡眠研究中心主任 Jerome Siegel 表示，证据显示，睡眠习惯可能并非由环境或文化决定，而是人类生理构造的核心特征。

source.text: These findings question the millions of dollars that have been spent on research that tries to explain why some sleepers get only about six hours of sleep a night.

translation.text: 这些发现令人质疑：为解释一些睡眠者为何每晚只睡约6小时而投入的数百万美元研究，是否建立在正确前提上。

source.text: Also, such findings question whether lack of sleep is a cause of obesity, mood disorders, and other physical and mental illnesses which have become so common in recent decades.

translation.text: 它们也让人怀疑，近几十年来日益常见的肥胖、情绪障碍以及其他身心疾病，是否真由睡眠不足引起。

source.text: Scientists have documented that people’s energy often falls in the mid-afternoon.

translation.text: 科学家已经记录到，人们的精力往往会在下午中段下降。

source.text: Some have suggested that it’s because we’ve managed to suppress a natural desire for a nap.

translation.text: 有人认为，这是因为我们设法压制了自然产生的午睡欲望。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: However, the new study provides evidence that this is unlikely, and that napping was actually rare in hunter-gatherer societies. The researchers estimated that naps may have occurred on up to 7 percent of winter days and 22 percent of summer days. They noted that their devices were only good at detecting longer naps, so it is possible that some of the study subjects took naps that were short, perhaps 15 minutes or less.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 然而，新研究提供的证据表明，这种说法不太可能成立，而且狩猎采集社会实际上很少有人午睡。研究人员估计，冬季最多有7%的日子可能出现午睡，夏季则最多为22%。他们也指出，所用设备只能较好地探测较长时间的午睡，因此部分研究对象可能短暂睡过一会儿，时间或许只有15分钟，甚至更短。

source.text: However, the new study provides evidence that this is unlikely, and that napping was actually rare in hunter-gatherer societies.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Another fascinating finding from the study had to do with the circadian rhythms, our daily activity cycles related to sunlight. Instead of going to sleep right at dusk, tribespeople were staying awake an average of between 2.5 and 4.4 hours after sunset. All three tribes had fires going, but the light itself was much lower than you might get from a light bulb. They did, however, have a tendency to wake up anywhere between an hour before and an hour after sunrise.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The tribespeople are also much healthier. Not a single one is overweight, indicating their overall higher levels of physical fitness. source.text: Socotra Island

translation.text: 索科特拉岛

headerUnits.sourceNormalizedText: Situated in the Arabian Sea off the Arabian Peninsula is the Socotra archipelago, a remnant of an ancient landmass that became separated from Africa and Arabia 18 million years ago.
headerUnits.translationNormalizedText: 索科特拉群岛位于阿拉伯半岛外的阿拉伯海，是一片古老陆块的残余；这片陆块在1,800万年前与非洲和阿拉伯分离。

source.text: Situated in the Arabian Sea off the Arabian Peninsula is the Socotra archipelago, a remnant of an ancient landmass that became separated from Africa and Arabia 18 million years ago.

translation.text: 索科特拉群岛位于阿拉伯半岛外的阿拉伯海，是一片古老陆块的残余；这片陆块在1,800万年前与非洲和阿拉伯分离。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: When scientists began the first substantial exploration of the islands 30 years ago, they found a fascinating collection of unusual plants and animals - a unique combination of 'relict' populations (organisms that have become extinct elsewhere) and species that have evolved to cope with the island's harsh conditions. In fact, almost a third of its plant species and up to 80 percent of its terrestrial animals are found nowhere else.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 30年前，科学家首次开始对这些岛屿进行大规模考察，发现了一批引人入胜的奇特动植物：这里既有独特的“残遗”种群（在其他地方已经灭绝的生物），也有为适应岛上严酷条件而演化出的物种。事实上，岛上近三分之一的植物物种和多达80%的陆生动物，在世界其他地方都找不到。

source.text: When scientists began the first substantial exploration of the islands 30 years ago, they found a fascinating collection of unusual plants and animals - a unique combination of 'relict' populations (organisms that have become extinct elsewhere) and species that have evolved to cope with the island's harsh conditions.

translation.text: 30年前，科学家首次开始对这些岛屿进行大规模考察，发现了一批引人入胜的奇特动植物：这里既有独特的“残遗”种群（在其他地方已经灭绝的生物），也有为适应岛上严酷条件而演化出的物种。

source.text: In fact, almost a third of its plant species and up to 80 percent of its terrestrial animals are found nowhere else.

translation.text: 事实上，岛上近三分之一的植物物种和多达80%的陆生动物，在世界其他地方都找不到。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Life in the arid conditions is harsh for the people living there too. Isolated from the mainland by hundreds of kilometres, and with monsoons that rage for several months every year, the islanders were historically self-sufficient - relying only on what they themselves could produce to survive. There are floods and droughts, and many islanders lack adequate water resources and nutrition. Medical care and education are limited.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 对当地居民来说，在这种干旱环境中生活同样艰苦。岛屿与大陆相隔数百公里，而且每年都有持续数月的猛烈季风，因此岛民过去一直自给自足，只能依靠自己生产的物资生存。这里既有洪水，也有干旱；许多岛民缺少充足的水资源和营养，医疗和教育也很有限。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: However, the main island, Socotra, is experiencing significant change. A rapid development programme has been instituted that will have far-reaching impacts on the island's people and the environment for decades to come. In the past, the only way to get to Socotra was by travelling for several days on a boat, but irregular flights began touching down on dirt landing strips during the late 1960s. By 1999, a runway had been constructed on Socotra that was capable of taking larger aircraft all year round, and since 2000 the capital, Hadibo, has seen huge expansion. New schools have been built, and a modern terminal was added to the airport, through which an increasing number of tourists are beginning to pass. And there are plans to construct new harbour facilities that will enable fishermen to sell their catch more easily, and also make it simpler for local people to have food, and bricks and timber for construction projects brought to the island.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 然而，主岛索科特拉岛正在经历重大变化。一项快速发展计划已经启动，未来几十年都将对岛上居民和环境产生深远影响。过去，前往索科特拉的唯一方式是乘船航行数日；到20世纪60年代后期，才有班次不固定的航班开始在土质跑道上降落。1999年，岛上建成了一条全年都能供大型飞机起降的跑道；自2000年以来，首府哈迪布大规模扩张。新学校已经落成，机场也增设了现代化航站楼，开始有越来越多游客经此出入。此外，岛上还计划新建港口设施，让渔民更容易出售渔获，也让居民更方便地把食品以及建筑工程所需的砖块和木材运到岛上。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: However, although these improvements are significant, it’s the continuing development of Socotra’s road system that is having the greatest impact on the islanders. Until 1991, a few dirt tracks, navigable only by four-wheel drive, gave access to part of the island. Otherwise it was only possible to reach most areas on foot, or with a donkey. By 2001, however, there was an extensive network of unpaved car tracks, and the following year a tarmac road, the first of its kind on Socotra, connecting the airport to Hadibo, was completed. Now, a road traverses the Diksam plateau and continues on to the south coast, making essential services more accessible to a large number of villagers.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 不过，尽管这些改善十分显著，对岛民影响最大的还是索科特拉公路系统的持续发展。直到1991年，岛上只有几条必须驾驶四轮驱动车才能通行的土路，只能到达部分地区；除此之外，前往大多数地方只能步行或骑驴。可是到2001年，岛上已有广泛的未铺装车道网络。第二年，索科特拉第一条柏油路完工，把机场与哈迪布连接起来。如今，一条公路横穿 Diksam 高原并继续通往南部海岸，使许多村民更容易获得基本服务。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: There is no doubt that the development of Socotra’s infrastructure has brought many benefits to the island's inhabitants, but there is growing concern that the speed with which it is taking place is so rapid that it will be difficult for local people to maintain certain traditions. There is also the fear that the developments will threaten the island's unique ecosystems. Building new roads and harbours may lead to the introduction of alien species to Socotra Island (as has already happened with the Indian house crow), damage to the sea's biodiversity through the increased collection and sale of coral, and tourist developments on an inappropriate and unsustainable scale.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 毫无疑问，索科特拉的基础设施建设给岛民带来了许多好处；但人们越来越担心，建设推进得如此迅速，当地居民将很难维持某些传统。人们也担心，这些开发会威胁岛上独特的生态系统。修建新道路和港口可能把外来物种带入索科特拉岛（印度家鸦已经是一个先例）；珊瑚采集和销售增加，可能破坏海洋生物多样性；旅游开发也可能达到不恰当且不可持续的规模。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Problems were also caused by increasing access to sensitive areas. For example, cutting the road along the coast caused considerable damage to the stunning scenery. However, some steps were then taken to limit the damage caused by further development. For example, biodiversity project officers were consulted in the planning stages of the road that crosses the centre of Socotra, so it avoids some of the most scenic areas and sites that contain plants only found in a limited number of locations. It is an area which is also home to the greatest concentrations of dragon's blood trees and supports many endemic animals.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: An agreement has now been reached about all future construction of roads. blocks.sourceNormalizedText: It wasn’t until five years ago that it all made sense. That was when Hodes was diagnosed with prosopagnosia, a condition that means he is unable to recognise faces. According to researchers, he is far from alone. In fact, the condition is not that uncommon, but until a few years ago only a few dozen cases had ever been described, and all of these had been caused by brain injury. Recently, though, researchers identified a second form of face blindness, developmental prosopagnosia, which is either present from birth or develops very early in life.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: It seems that if you have never known what it is to recognise a face, you don’t necessarily know that you are supposed to be able to. Prosopagnosics almost always know that they have trouble recognising people, but they often don’t realise that other people have better recognition skills than they do, says Brad Duchaine, a researcher at UCL.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Despite these issues, the majority of developmental prosopagnosics possess strategies that allow them to get around their difficulty—for instance, by recognising hair, clothing, or a person’s way of speaking—so, unless they see a familiar person out of context, with a new hairstyle or in different clothes, they can recognise people just fine. Even so, the discovery of developmental prosopagnosia has attracted attention from neuroscientists keen to discover what is different about the brain of face-blind people. This difference, they believe, could help solve the problem of how the brain deals with information in general, not just visual data. In other words, it may show whether the brain has specialised parts for specific tasks or is more of a general-purpose information processor.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 尽管存在这些问题，大多数发育性面孔失认症患者都有办法绕过这一困难，例如通过发型、衣着或说话方式来认人。因此，除非在脱离平时熟悉情境的场合遇到熟人，或对方换了新发型或穿着不同，否则他们通常都能顺利认出对方。即便如此，发育性面孔失认症的发现仍引起了神经科学家的关注，他们很想弄清脸盲者的大脑究竟有何不同。研究人员认为，这种差异可能有助于解释大脑通常如何处理信息，而不只是如何处理视觉数据。换句话说，它或许能说明，大脑是否存在分别负责特定任务的专门区域，还是更像一个通用的信息处理器。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: One issue, however, that will present challenges for researchers is that no two prosopagnosics are the same. Some have problems only with faces, while others have trouble with ordinary everyday objects and, so it turns out, animals which would normally be familiar as well. Some prosopagnosics can train themselves to recognise specific faces; others can’t even recognise their own in a mirror. When some have been tested they could identify the emotion that was conveyed on another’s face, even though the face itself seemed unfamiliar, while for other subjects this was an impossibility. Some cannot recognise the faces of old friends or fellow students but have no trouble telling whether a particular face from such groups would be attractive to most people. Because of this diversity, working out the cause of prosopagnosia will not be easy.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 不过，研究人员将面临的一项挑战是，没有两名面孔失认症患者的情况完全相同。有些人只难以辨别人脸，另一些人则连普通日常物品，甚至通常应该很熟悉的动物也难以识别。有些患者可以通过训练认出某几张特定面孔，另一些人却连镜中的自己都认不出来。测试发现，有些人虽然觉得一张脸很陌生，却能识别那张脸表达的情绪；而另一些受试者完全做不到。有些人认不出老朋友或同学的脸，却能轻松判断这类人中的某一张脸是否会被大多数人视为好看。由于存在如此多样的情况，要查明面孔失认症的病因并不容易。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: In Martina Gruter’s study, the prosopagnosics who agreed to have their parents and relatives tested reported at least one relative with the condition. Having looked at 38 cases in seven families, the German team believe they have good evidence that a single gene could be responsible. Duchaine also has some evidence that face blindness could be inherited but thinks other factors might be more significant. He refers to studies of babies born with a condition which means the eye’s lens is not clear, and when it’s the left one, being unable to see through this eye during the first two months of life is a major risk factor for prosopagnosia.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Whatever the cause, what most prosopagnosics want to know is whether they can do anything to improve their face-recognition skills. Joseph DeGutis, a graduate student at the University of California, recently reported successfully training a severe developmental prosopagnosic to recognise faces during tests carried out in the laboratory. The subject also reported that recognising faces in everyday life became easier due to the training. Duchaine now plans to attempt to train sufferers to recognise the five people they most need to know—maybe their immediate family, for example, and essential colleagues. Thomas Gruter, Martina Gruter’s husband, who also works on her team, however, is not convinced it will work. ‘I don’t know how you can have more training than you have already had,’ he says. ‘Humans already spend all day looking at faces.’ He also points out that cheating is a possibility during tests and provides an example. One person we studied said that when she was doing the face-recognition test, she memorised the distance between nose and upper lip. She wasn’t the only one. So you can perform well in the test and not do so well in real life.

translation.text: 悉尼歌剧院

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Sydney Opera House is an example of late modern architecture; it is admired internationally and treasured by the people of Australia.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 悉尼歌剧院是晚期现代建筑的典范；它在国际上广受赞赏，也深受澳大利亚人民珍爱。

source.text: Sydney Opera House is an example of late modern architecture; it is admired internationally and treasured by the people of Australia.

translation.text: 悉尼歌剧院是晚期现代建筑的典范；它在国际上广受赞赏，也深受澳大利亚人民珍爱。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: In 1956 the Premier of New South Wales, Australia, announced an international competition for the design of an opera house for Sydney. It attracted more than 200 entries from around the world and was won by Jørn Utzon, a relatively little-known architect from Denmark. The story goes that during the judging of the competition, one judge, American architect Eero Saarinen, arrived in Sydney after the other three judges had started assessing the entries. He looked through their rejected entries and stopped at the Utzon design, declaring it to be outstanding.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 1956年，澳大利亚新南威尔士州州长宣布举行一场国际竞赛，为悉尼歌剧院征集设计方案。竞赛收到来自世界各地的200多份参赛作品，最终获胜的是当时相对不太知名的丹麦建筑师 Jørn Utzon。故事是这样的：评审竞赛方案时，另外3名评委已经开始评选，美国建筑师 Eero Saarinen 才抵达悉尼。他翻看了其他评委淘汰的作品，看到 Utzon 的设计时停了下来，并宣布这一方案出类拔萃。

source.text: In 1956 the Premier of New South Wales, Australia, announced an international competition for the design of an opera house for Sydney.

translation.text: 1956年，澳大利亚新南威尔士州州长宣布举行一场国际竞赛，为悉尼歌剧院征集设计方案。

source.text: It attracted more than 200 entries from around the world and was won by Jørn Utzon, a relatively little-known architect from Denmark.

translation.text: 竞赛收到来自世界各地的200多份参赛作品，最终获胜的是当时相对不太知名的丹麦建筑师 Jørn Utzon。

source.text: The story goes that during the judging of the competition, one judge, American architect Eero Saarinen, arrived in Sydney after the other three judges had started assessing the entries.

translation.text: 故事是这样的：评审竞赛方案时，另外3名评委已经开始评选，美国建筑师 Eero Saarinen 才抵达悉尼。

source.text: He looked through their rejected entries and stopped at the Utzon design, declaring it to be outstanding.

translation.text: 他翻看了其他评委淘汰的作品，看到 Utzon 的设计时停了下来，并宣布这一方案出类拔萃。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: It was Utzon’s life and travels that had shaped his design for the Sydney Opera House. Though he had never visited the site, he used his maritime background to study naval charts of Sydney Harbour. His early exposure to shipbuilding provided the inspiration for the design of the roof, which is a series of curved ‘shells’ that look like the sails of a sailing ship billowing in the wind. From his travels to Mexico, he had the idea of placing his building on a wide horizontal platform.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: Utzon 的人生经历和旅行塑造了他对悉尼歌剧院的设计。尽管从未到过建筑所在地，他仍利用自己的航海背景研究悉尼港海图。早年接触造船的经历给了他屋顶设计的灵感：屋顶由一系列弧形“壳体”组成，看起来就像帆船的船帆在风中鼓起。他在墨西哥旅行后，又产生了把建筑安置在一座宽阔水平平台上的想法。

source.text: It was Utzon’s life and travels that had shaped his design for the Sydney Opera House.

translation.text: Utzon 的人生经历和旅行塑造了他对悉尼歌剧院的设计。

source.text: Though he had never visited the site, he used his maritime background to study naval charts of Sydney Harbour.

translation.text: 尽管从未到过建筑所在地，他仍利用自己的航海背景研究悉尼港海图。

source.text: His early exposure to shipbuilding provided the inspiration for the design of the roof, which is a series of curved ‘shells’ that look like the sails of a sailing ship billowing in the wind.

translation.text: 他在墨西哥旅行后，又产生了把建筑安置在一座宽阔水平平台上的想法。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Construction of the platform began in 1959, and throughout the early 1960s Utzon amended his original designs in order to develop a way to build the large ‘shells’ that cover the two main halls. The construction of the roof brought together some of the world’s best engineers and craftsmen, devising innovative techniques to create a major visual impact in accordance with Utzon’s vision. The design was one of the first examples of the use of computer-aided design for complex shapes.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 平台于1959年动工。在整个20世纪60年代初期，Utzon 不断修改原始设计，以找到建造覆盖两座主厅的大型“壳体”的办法。屋顶建设汇集了世界上一些最优秀的工程师和工匠；他们设计出创新技术，以实现 Utzon 设想的强烈视觉效果。这项设计也是最早运用计算机辅助设计处理复杂形状的实例之一。

translation.text: 平台于1959年动工。在整个20世纪60年代初期，Utzon 不断修改原始设计，以找到建造覆盖两座主厅的大型“壳体”的办法。

translation.text: 这项设计也是最早运用计算机辅助设计处理复杂形状的实例之一。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Although Utzon had spectacular plans for the interior, he was unable to realise them. Cost overruns contributed to criticism of the project and, after a change of government, the Minister of Works began questioning Utzon’s schedules and cost estimates. Payments to Utzon were stopped and he was forced to withdraw as chief architect in 1966. Following his resignation, there were protests through the streets led by prominent architect Harry Seidler and others, demanding that Utzon be reinstated as architect. However, Utzon was not reinstated and left Australia in 1966. He never returned, and new architects were appointed to complete the building in his absence. The original cost estimate for the Opera House was $7 million, with the completion date set for 26 January 1963. However, the Opera House was not formally completed until 1973, having cost $102 million.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: Utzon 虽然为内部空间制订了宏伟方案，却没能将其实现。成本超支加剧了人们对项目的批评；政府换届后，工程部长开始质疑 Utzon 的进度安排和成本估算。付给 Utzon 的款项被停止，他于1966年被迫辞去首席建筑师职务。Utzon 辞职后，著名建筑师 Harry Seidler 等人带领民众走上街头抗议，要求恢复 Utzon 的建筑师职位。然而，他并未获复职，并于1966年离开澳大利亚，此后再也没有回来。新的建筑师受命在他缺席的情况下完成建筑。歌剧院最初预计耗资$700万，计划于1963年1月26日完工。然而，歌剧院直到1973年才正式竣工，最终耗资$1.02亿。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Since its opening in 1973, Sydney Opera House has earned a reputation as a world-class performing-arts centre and become a symbol of both Sydney and Australia. Situated at Bennelong Point on Sydney Harbour, it consists of a series of large precast ‘shells’ made of concrete, each composed of sections of a sphere of 75.2 metres radius, forming the roofs of the structure, set on a monumental platform. The building is 183 metres long and 120 metres wide at its widest point. It is supported on 588 concrete piers, which are sunk approximately 25 metres below sea level.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 悉尼歌剧院自1973年开放以来，赢得了世界一流表演艺术中心的声誉，也成为悉尼和澳大利亚共同的象征。它位于悉尼港的贝尼朗角，由一系列大型预制混凝土“壳体”组成；每个壳体都由半径75.2米的球面片组成，共同构成建筑屋顶，并坐落在一座宏伟平台上。建筑长183米，最宽处120米，由588根混凝土桩支撑；这些桩深入海平面以下约25米。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Although the roof structures are commonly referred to as ‘shells’, they are precast concrete panels supported by concrete ribs. The ‘shells’ are covered with 1,056,006 white and cream-coloured tiles manufactured in a factory in Sweden that generally produced stoneware tiles for the paper-mill industry. The design solution and construction of the shell structure took eight years to complete, and the development of the special ceramic tiles took over three years. Apart from the tiles covering the ‘shells’, the building’s exterior is mostly clad with granite quarried in Australia.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 屋顶结构虽然通常被称为“壳体”，实际却是由混凝土肋条支撑的预制混凝土板。这些“壳体”表面覆盖着1,056,006块白色和米黄色瓷砖，产自瑞典一家通常为造纸厂制造粗陶砖的工厂。壳体结构的设计方案和施工花了8年才完成，特制陶瓷砖的研发则用了3年多。除覆盖“壳体”的瓷砖外，建筑外部大多包覆着在澳大利亚开采的花岗岩。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Contrary to its name, Sydney Opera House includes multiple performance venues. It is among the busiest performing-arts centres in the world, holding over 1,500 performances each year. It hosts a large number of performing-arts companies, including the four resident companies: Opera Australia, the Australian Ballet, the Sydney Theatre Company and the Sydney Symphony Orchestra.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 与名称给人的印象不同，悉尼歌剧院内设有多个演出场地。它是世界上最繁忙的表演艺术中心之一，每年举办1,500多场演出。这里接待众多表演艺术团体，其中包括4个常驻团体：澳大利亚歌剧团、澳大利亚芭蕾舞团、悉尼戏剧团和悉尼交响乐团。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: With its grand setting and cathedral-like atmosphere, the Concert Hall is Sydney Opera House’s most prestigious performance space. The largest of all interior venues, it delivers outstanding acoustics thanks to its high ceiling and wood panelling. There is a sizeable outdoor forecourt from which people ascend to the main entrance. The steps, which lead up from the forecourt to the main performance venues, are nearly 100 metres wide.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 音乐厅环境宏伟，氛围宛如大教堂，是悉尼歌剧院最负盛名的演出空间。它是所有室内场地中最大的一座，高耸的天花板和木质镶板带来了出色的音响效果。建筑外有一片宽阔的前庭广场，人们可从那里拾级而上进入主入口。从前庭广场通往主要演出场地的台阶宽近100米。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: In 1999 Utzon was re-engaged to develop a set of design principles to act as a guide for future changes to the building. All of this design work he did from his base in Europe. These principles help to ensure that the building’s architectural integrity is maintained. The first alteration to the exterior was the addition of a new colonnade, which shades nine large glass openings in the previously solid exterior wall. This Utzon-led project, completed in 2006, enabled theatre patrons to see the harbour for the first time from the theatre foyers. The design also incorporates the first public lift and interior escalators to assist less-mobile patrons.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 1999年，Utzon 再次受聘，制订一套设计原则，为建筑今后的改动提供指导。所有设计工作都是他在欧洲的工作地点完成的。这些原则有助于确保建筑在设计上的完整性得到保持。建筑外观的首次改动是增建一条新柱廊，为原先封闭的外墙上9处大型玻璃开口遮阳。这项由 Utzon 主持、于2006年完成的工程，使剧院观众首次能够从前厅看到海港。设计中还加入了首部公共电梯和室内自动扶梯，以方便行动不便的观众。

source.text: The Blockbuster Phenomenon

translation.text: “重磅展览”现象

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Museums in Australia, like other pleasure-giving public organizations, are adapting their activities so that they more closely reflect the marketplace.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 澳大利亚的博物馆和其他给公众带来乐趣的机构一样，正在调整自己的活动，使其更贴近市场。

source.text: Museums in Australia, like other pleasure-giving public organizations, are adapting their activities so that they more closely reflect the marketplace.

translation.text: 澳大利亚的博物馆和其他给公众带来乐趣的机构一样，正在调整自己的活动，使其更贴近市场。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Since the 1980s, the term ‘blockbuster’ has become the fashionable word for spectacular, high-profile museum exhibitions that have the ability to attract large crowds. A blockbuster is a ‘large-scale loan exhibition that people who normally don’t go to museums will stand in line for hours to see’ (Eisen 1984). Once the museum that created the exhibition has shown it to its local market, it can be offered to other organizations for a fee. This means that you can boost your own door takings and make money from boosting someone else’s door takings.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 自20世纪80年代以来，“blockbuster”一词开始流行起来，用来指场面壮观、备受瞩目、能够吸引大批观众的博物馆展览。重磅展览是“一种大型借展，连平时不去博物馆的人也愿意排上几小时队观看”（Eisen，1984）。策展博物馆先向本地市场展出，之后便可以收费提供给其他机构。这意味着，博物馆既能通过增加自己的门票收入获益，也能通过帮助其他机构增加门票收入来赚钱。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Museums across the UK, USA, Canada and Australia currently operate under a system of plural funding: revenue raised through contributions by federal, state and/or local governments, combined with revenue raised through admission charges and other activities. Maintaining and increasing visitor levels is thus paramount and involves not only creating or hiring blockbuster exhibitions, but providing regular exhibition changes and innovations. In addition, the visiting public have become known as customers rather than visitors, and the skills that are valued in museums to keep the new customers coming through the door have changed. Curators are now administrators, and being a museum director no longer requires an Arts degree—but public relations skills are essential if the museum is going to compete with other museums to stage travelling exhibitions which draw huge crowds.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 英国、美国、加拿大和澳大利亚各地的博物馆目前采用多元筹资体系：联邦、州和地方政府中一个或多个层级提供的资金，与门票及其他活动带来的收入结合起来。因此，维持并增加参观人数至关重要；这不仅需要创办或租入重磅展览，还需要定期更换展览并不断创新。此外，前来参观的公众开始被称为“顾客”，而不再是“参观者”；为了让这些新顾客不断走进博物馆，馆方所看重的技能也发生了变化。策展人如今成了管理人员，担任博物馆馆长也不再要求具备人文学科学位；不过，如果博物馆要与其他博物馆竞争举办吸引大批人群的巡回展览，公共关系技能必不可少。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The convergence of museums, the heritage industry, tourism, profit-making and pleasure-giving has resulted in the new ‘museology’. This has given rise to much debate about whether it is appropriate to see museums primarily as tourist attractions. In literature from both the UK and USA, the words that are starting to appear in some descriptions of blockbusters are ‘less scholarly’, ‘non-elitist’ and ‘popularist’, while others extol the virtues of encouraging scholars to co-operate on projects, and to provide exhibitions that cater for a broad selection of the community rather than an elite sector. Whatever commentators may think, managers of museums worldwide are looking for artful ways to blend culture and commerce, and blockbuster exhibitions are at the top of the list.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: But do blockbusters held in public institutions really create a surplus to fund other activities? If the bottom line is profit, then according to the records of many major museums blockbusters do make money. For museums in some countries, it may be the money that they require to replace parts of their collections or to fix buildings that are in need of attention. For some museums in Australia, it may be the opportunity to illustrate that they are attempting to pay their way by recovering part of their operating costs. Also, creating or hiring a blockbuster has many positive spin-offs: blockbusters mean crowds, and crowds are good for the local economy, providing increased trade for shops, hotels, restaurants, the transport industry and retailers. The argument that the arts provide sustained economic benefits has been well illustrated in impact studies in the USA and UK.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 然而，在公共机构举办的重磅展览，真的能产生盈余来资助其他活动吗？如果最终标准是利润，那么根据许多大型博物馆的记录，重磅展览确实能赚钱。对一些国家的博物馆来说，这笔钱可能是更新部分藏品或修缮需要维护的建筑所必需的。对澳大利亚的一些博物馆而言，这可能也是一个机会，用来表明它们正试图收回部分运营成本，靠自身努力承担开支。此外，创办或租入重磅展览会产生许多积极的连带效应：重磅展览会带来人群，而人群有利于当地经济，可以增加商店、酒店、餐馆、交通业和零售商的生意。美国和英国的影响研究已经充分说明，艺术能够带来持续的经济效益。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: However, blockbusters require large capital expenditure and draw on resources across all branches of an organization, and the costs don’t end there. There is a Human Resource Management cost in addition to a measurable ‘real’ dollar cost. Receiving a touring exhibition draws resources from across functional management structures in a project-management style. Everyone—from general labourers to building services, front-of-house, technical, promotional, educational and administrative staff—is required to perform additional tasks. Furthermore, as an increasing number of institutions try their hand at increasing visitor numbers and memberships (and therefore revenue) by staging blockbuster exhibitions, it may be less likely that blockbusters will continue to provide a surplus to subsidize other activities due to the competitive nature of the market.

Creating, mounting or hiring blockbusters is exhausting, with the real costs throughout an institution difficult to calculate. Secondly, as some analysts have argued, the ‘shopkeeping’ mentality and cost-benefit analysis, and a pure concentration on the bottom line, can squeeze substance out of an exhibition. blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Some discoveries are so unusual it takes decades and sometimes even centuries to understand their full significance. One such discovery is the fossil bed known as the Burgess Shale, which contains a record of bizarre creatures that lived 505 million years ago. It was discovered in the Canadian Rockies over a century ago, and was popularized in 1989 in a book, Wonderful Life, by Stephen Jay Gould, an American paleontologist.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The Burgess Shale fossils were created at a time when the future Canadian land mass was situated near the Earth’s equator. The creatures were preserved when an entire marine ecosystem was buried in mud that eventually hardened and became exposed hundreds of millions of years later in an outcrop of the Rocky Mountains. American paleontologist Charles Walcott, following reports of fabulous fossil finds by construction workers on a Canadian railway who were digging in the mountains in the late 19th century, is said to have tripped over a block of shale in 1909 that revealed the area’s remarkable supply of specimens. It has long been believed that the curious fauna that lived there vanished in a series of extinctions because the fossil record ends abruptly. But that no longer appears to be the case.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 伯吉斯页岩化石形成时，日后成为加拿大的陆块位于地球赤道附近。整个海洋生态系统被泥浆掩埋，这些生物因而保存下来；泥浆最终变硬，又在数亿年后作为落基山脉的一处露头暴露出来。19世纪后期，在山中修建加拿大铁路的工人报告发现了极为惊人的化石。美国古生物学家 Charles Walcott 随后前往当地；据说，他在1909年被一块页岩绊了一下，由此发现这一地区蕴藏着数量惊人的标本。长期以来，人们一直认为，生活在这里的奇特动物群经历了一连串灭绝，因为化石记录突然中断。不过，现在看来事实似乎并非如此。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The Burgess Shale began to form soon after a period known as the Cambrian explosion, when most major groups of complex animals arose over a surprisingly short period. Before 560 million years ago, most living things were either individual cells or simple colonies of cells. Then, and for reasons that remain a mystery, life massively diversified and became ever more complex as the rate of evolution increased. An unusual feature of the Burgess Shale is that it is one of the earliest fossil beds to contain impressions of soft body parts alongside the remains of bones and shells, which is highly unusual.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Paleontologists had long thought that many of the Burgess Shale animals were examples of experiments in evolution. blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Now another misconception has been quashed. Writing in Nature recently, Peter Van Roy of Yale University in the United States and his colleagues suggest that the sudden absence of such crazy soft-bodied fossils does not indicate a mass extinction, but merely an end to the unusual local circumstances that caused the creatures to be preserved. In an area of the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, Van Roy’s team of researchers has found another diverse (and sometimes bizarre) assemblage of soft-bodied organisms from a period after the Burgess Shale was formed. One discovery includes something that may be a stalked barnacle. This suggests that the evolution of such complex life went on uninterrupted. For its part, the Burgess Shale continues to produce an astonishing array of indefinable creatures faster than paleontologists can examine them. source.text: The Clipper Races

translation.text: 飞剪船竞赛

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the British East India Company had the monopoly on trade with China and India. This meant that because no rival could legally import tea or other goods from these countries at this time, the company was rarely in a hurry to transport its merchandise. Instead, its priority was to minimise costs by carrying as much as possible on each ship. This meant that its ships – known as East Indiamen – were enormous, strong and very slow.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: In fact it was the Americans who pioneered the first clipper ships. These vessels were fast and slender, with a narrow hull that was deeper at the back than at the front, and masses of sails on tall masts. They earned their name from the way that they ‘clipped off’ journey time. British merchants resolved to build their own clippers to rival the Americans, and the first British tea clipper, Stornaway, was built in Aberdeen in 1850. More tea clippers were designed and built in Britain throughout the 1850s and 1860s; they had a narrower beam than their American equivalents, making them less powerful during storms but faster in calmer weather.

source.text: The Development of Plastics

translation.text: 塑料的发展

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The first plastics were developed as a substitute for natural rubber. Chemically, rubber is a polymer—a compound containing large molecules that are formed by the bonding of many smaller, simpler units, repeated over and over again. The same bonding principle—polymerization—is the basis of the creation of a huge range of plastics by the chemical industry.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 最早的塑料是作为天然橡胶的替代品开发出来的。从化学角度看，橡胶是一种聚合物，也就是由许多较小、较简单的单元反复连接，形成大分子的化合物。同样的连接原理——聚合反应——也是化学工业制造种类繁多的塑料的基础。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The first plastic was developed as a result of a competition in the USA. In the 1860s, $10,000 was offered to anybody who could replace ivory—supplies of which were declining—with something equally good as a material for making billiard balls. The prize was won by John Wesley Hyatt, with a material called celluloid. Celluloid was made by dissolving cellulose, a carbohydrate obtained from plants, in a solution of camphor dissolved in ethanol. This new material rapidly found other applications in the manufacture of everyday products such as knife handles and detachable collars and cuffs. But perhaps the best-known celluloid product was photographic film, without which the film industry could never have taken off at the end of the 19th century.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Celluloid can be repeatedly softened and reshaped by heat, and is known as a thermoplastic. In 1907, Leo Baekeland (1863–1944), a Belgian chemist working in the USA, invented a different kind of plastic by causing phenol and formaldehyde to react together. Baekeland called it Bakelite, and it was the first of the thermosets—plastics that can be cast and moulded while hot, but cannot be softened by heat and reshaped once they have set. Bakelite was a good insulator, and was resistant to water and acid. With these properties it was soon being used in the manufacture of electrical switches as well as a variety of domestic items.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: As the century went on, the range of newly developed plastics increased. Chemists began looking for other small molecules that could be strung together to make polymers. In the 1930s, chemists in Britain discovered that the gas ethylene would polymerize under heat and pressure to form a thermoplastic they called polythene. Polypropylene followed in the 1950s. Both are used to make bottles, pipes and plastic bags. A small change in the starting material—replacing a hydrogen atom in ethylene with a chlorine atom—produced rigid PVC (polyvinyl chloride), a fireproof plastic suitable for drains and gutters. By adding certain chemicals, a soft form of PVC can be produced, suitable as a substitute for rubber in items such as waterproof clothing. A closely related plastic is Teflon or PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene). It produces very little friction, making it ideal for products such as non-stick frying pans.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 随着20世纪向前发展，新开发的塑料种类不断增加。化学家开始寻找其他可以串联起来形成聚合物的小分子。20世纪30年代，英国化学家发现，乙烯气体在加热和加压条件下会发生聚合，形成一种他们称为聚乙烯的热塑性塑料。20世纪50年代，聚丙烯也随之问世。这两种材料都用于制造瓶子、管道和塑料袋。只要略微改变起始材料——把乙烯中的一个氢原子换成氯原子——就能制成硬质PVC（聚氯乙烯）；这种塑料防火，适合制作排水管和檐沟。加入某些化学物质后，还可以制成软质PVC，用于替代防水服等物品中的橡胶。与之关系密切的另一种塑料是 Teflon，也称 PTFE（聚四氟乙烯）。它产生的摩擦很小，非常适合用于不粘煎锅等产品。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: In the 1930s, the first of the man-made fibres was created—nylon. Its inventor was a chemist called Wallace Carothers (1896–1937), who worked for the Du Pont company in the USA. He found that under the right conditions two particular chemicals would form a polymer that could be pumped out through holes and then stretched to form long glossy threads that could be woven like silk. Its first use was to make parachutes for the US armed forces in World War II. In the postwar years, it completely replaced silk in the manufacture of stockings.

passages.title: The Development of The Silk Industry

headerUnits.sourceNormalizedText: The Development of The Silk Industry

source.text: The Development of The Silk Industry

translation.text: 丝绸业的发展

headerUnits.sourceNormalizedText: Silk, a natural fibre produced by a particular worm called a silkworm, has been used in clothing for many centuries.
headerUnits.translationNormalizedText: 丝绸是一种由蚕吐出的天然纤维，数百年来一直用于制作衣物。

source.text: Silk, a natural fibre produced by a particular worm called a silkworm, has been used in clothing for many centuries.

translation.text: 丝绸是一种由蚕吐出的天然纤维，数百年来一直用于制作衣物。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: When silk was first discovered in China over 4,500 years ago, it was reserved exclusively for the use of the emperor, his close relations and the very highest of his dignitaries. Within the palace, the emperor is believed to have worn a robe of white silk; outside, he, his principal wife, and the heir to the throne wore yellow, the colour of the earth.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 4,500多年前，丝绸刚在中国被发现时，只供皇帝、皇帝的近亲和地位最高的显贵使用。据认为，在宫内，皇帝身穿白色丝袍；在宫外，皇帝、正妻和皇位继承人则穿黄色丝袍；黄色是大地的颜色。

source.text: When silk was first discovered in China over 4,500 years ago, it was reserved exclusively for the use of the emperor, his close relations and the very highest of his dignitaries.

translation.text: 4,500多年前，丝绸刚在中国被发现时，只供皇帝、皇帝的近亲和地位最高的显贵使用。

source.text: Within the palace, the emperor is believed to have worn a robe of white silk; outside, he, his principal wife, and the heir to the throne wore yellow, the colour of the earth.

translation.text: 据认为，在宫内，皇帝身穿白色丝袍；在宫外，皇帝、正妻和皇位继承人则穿黄色丝袍；黄色是大地的颜色。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Gradually silk came into more general use, and the various classes of Chinese society began wearing tunics of silk. As well as being used for clothing and decoration, silk was quite quickly put to industrial use, and rapidly became one of the principal elements of the Chinese economy. It was used in the production of musical instruments, as string for fishing, and even as the world’s first luxury paper. Eventually even the common people were able to wear garments of silk.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 渐渐地，丝绸的使用范围扩大，中国社会的各个阶层开始穿丝质长袍。丝绸除了用于服装和装饰，也很快进入工业用途，并迅速成为中国经济的主要组成部分之一。它被用来制作乐器、鱼线，甚至成为世界上最早的高级纸张。最终，普通百姓也能穿上丝绸衣物。

source.text: Gradually silk came into more general use, and the various classes of Chinese society began wearing tunics of silk.

source.text: As well as being used for clothing and decoration, silk was quite quickly put to industrial use, and rapidly became one of the principal elements of the Chinese economy.

source.text: It was used in the production of musical instruments, as string for fishing, and even as the world’s first luxury paper.

translation.text: 它被用来制作乐器、鱼线，甚至成为世界上最早的高级纸张。

source.text: Eventually even the common people were able to wear garments of silk.

translation.text: 最终，普通百姓也能穿上丝绸衣物。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: During the Han dynasty (206 BC-220 AD), silk ceased to be a mere fabric and became a form of currency. Farmers paid their taxes in grain and silk, and silk was used to pay civil servants and to reward subjects for outstanding services. Values were calculated in lengths of silk as they had previously been calculated in weight of gold. Before long, silk became a currency used in trade with foreign countries, which continued into the Tang dynasty (616-907 AD). It is possible that this added importance was the result of a major increase in production. Silk also found its way so thoroughly into the Chinese language that 230 of the 5,000 most common characters of Mandarin have ‘silk’ as their key component.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 汉朝时期（公元前206年—公元220年），丝绸不再只是一种织物，还成为货币。农民用谷物和丝绸缴税，丝绸也被用来给官员发放报酬，并奖励功绩卓越的臣民。物品的价值此前以黄金重量计算，此时则按丝绸的长度计算。不久，丝绸成为与外国贸易时使用的货币，这种情况一直延续到唐朝（公元616—907年）。丝绸地位的提高，可能是产量大幅增加的结果。丝绸还深深进入了汉语：普通话中最常用的5,000个汉字里，有230个以“丝”为关键组成部分。

source.text: During the Han dynasty (206 BC-220 AD), silk ceased to be a mere fabric and became a form of currency.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Silk became a precious commodity, highly sought after by other countries from an early date, and it is believed that the silk trade actually existed before the Silk Road was officially opened in the second century BC. An Egyptian mummy with a silk thread in her hair, dating from 1070 BC, has been discovered in the village of Deir el Medina near the Valley of the Kings, and is probably the earliest evidence of the silk trade. During the second century BC, the Chinese emperor Han Wu Di’s ambassadors travelled as far west as Persia and Mesopotamia, bearing gifts including silks. A range of important finds of Chinese silks have also been made along the Silk Road. One of the most dramatic of these finds was some Tang silk discovered in 1900. It is believed that around 1015 AD Buddhist monks, possibly alarmed by the threat of invasion by Tibetan people, had sealed more than ten thousand manuscripts and silk paintings, silk banners and textiles in caves near Dunhuang, a trading station on the Silk Road in north-west China.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 丝绸很早就成为其他国家竞相求购的珍贵商品。人们认为，丝绸贸易其实早在公元前2世纪丝绸之路正式开通前就已存在。在帝王谷附近的代尔麦迪纳村，人们发现了一具头发中带有一根丝线的埃及木乃伊，其年代可追溯到公元前1070年；这或许是丝绸贸易最早的证据。公元前2世纪，汉武帝的使者携带包括丝绸在内的礼物，一路向西到达波斯和美索不达米亚。丝绸之路沿线还出土了许多重要的中国丝绸遗物，其中最引人注目的发现之一，是1900年出土的一批唐代丝绸。据认为，大约在公元1015年，佛教僧侣可能因担忧西藏人入侵，将一万多份手稿以及丝绸画、丝幡和丝织品封存在敦煌附近的洞窟中；敦煌是中国西北部丝绸之路上的一处贸易站。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Some historians believe the first Europeans to set eyes upon the fabulous fabric were the Roman legions of Marcus Licinius Crassus, Governor of Syria. According to certain accounts of the period, at an important battle near the Euphrates River in 53 BC, the Roman soldiers were so startled by the bright silken banners of the enemy that they fled in panic. Yet, within decades Chinese silks were widely worn by the rich and noble families of Rome. The Roman Emperor Heliogabalus (218-222 AD) wore nothing but silk. By 380 AD, the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus reported that the use of silk, which was once confined to the nobility, had now spread to all classes without distinction—even to the lowest. The desire for silk continued to increase over the centuries. Despite this demand, the price of silk remained very high.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 一些历史学家认为，最早亲眼见到这种奇异织物的欧洲人，是叙利亚总督 Marcus Licinius Crassus 统领的罗马军团。根据当时的某些记载，公元前53年，幼发拉底河附近的一场重要战役中，罗马士兵被敌人鲜艳的丝质旗帜惊得仓皇逃跑。然而，几十年后，丝绸已在罗马富裕的贵族家庭中广泛穿用。罗马皇帝 Heliogabalus（公元218—222年）只穿丝绸衣物。到公元380年，罗马历史学家 Ammianus Marcellinus 记载，丝绸过去只限贵族使用，如今已不分等级地传播到所有阶层，甚至包括社会最底层。几个世纪里，人们对丝绸的需求不断增长。尽管需求旺盛，丝绸价格始终很高。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: In spite of their secrecy about production methods, the Chinese eventually lost their monopoly on silk production. Knowledge of silk production methods reached Korea around 200 BC, when waves of Chinese immigrants arrived there. Shortly after 300 AD, it travelled westward, and the cultivation of the silkworm was established in India.

source.text: In spite of their secrecy about production methods, the Chinese eventually lost their monopoly on silk production.

source.text: Shortly after 300 AD, it travelled westward, and the cultivation of the silkworm was established in India.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Around 550 AD silk production reached the Middle East. Records indicate that two monks from Constantinople (modern-day Istanbul), capital of the Byzantine Empire, appeared at their emperor’s court with silkworm eggs which they had obtained secretly, and hidden in their hollow bamboo walking sticks. Under their supervision the eggs hatched into worms, and the worms spun silk threads. Byzantium was in the silk business at last. The Byzantine church and state created imperial workshops, monopolising production and keeping the secret to themselves. This allowed a silk industry to be established, undercutting the market for ordinary-grade Chinese silk. However, high quality silk textiles, woven in China especially for the Middle Eastern market, continued to achieve high prices in the West, and trade along the Silk Road continued as before. By the sixth century the Persians, too, had mastered the art of silk weaving, developing their own rich patterns and techniques. But it wasn’t until the 13th century that Italy began silk production, with the introduction of 2,000 skilled silk weavers from Constantinople. Eventually, silk production became widespread throughout Europe.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 大约公元550年，丝绸生产技术传到中东。记载显示，两名来自拜占庭帝国首都君士坦丁堡（今伊斯坦布尔）的僧侣来到皇帝宫廷，带来了他们秘密取得并藏在空心竹手杖中的蚕卵。在两人的照料下，蚕卵孵化成蚕，蚕又吐出丝线。拜占庭终于进入丝绸行业。拜占庭的教会和国家设立了皇家作坊，垄断生产，并严守其中的秘密。丝绸业由此建立起来，挤占了普通等级中国丝绸的市场。不过，中国专为中东市场织造的优质丝绸，在西方仍能卖出高价，丝绸之路上的贸易也照旧继续。到6世纪，波斯人也掌握了丝绸织造技术，并发展出自己华丽的图案和工艺。但直到13世纪，随着2,000名来自君士坦丁堡的熟练丝织工到来，意大利才开始生产丝绸。最终，丝绸生产遍及欧洲。

source.text: Around 550 AD silk production reached the Middle East.

translation.text: 大约公元550年，丝绸生产技术传到中东。

source.text: Records indicate that two monks from Constantinople (modern-day Istanbul), capital of the Byzantine Empire, appeared at their emperor’s court with silkworm eggs which they had obtained secretly, and hidden in their hollow bamboo walking sticks.

translation.text: 记载显示，两名来自拜占庭帝国首都君士坦丁堡（今伊斯坦布尔）的僧侣来到皇帝宫廷，带来了他们秘密取得并藏在空心竹手杖中的蚕卵。

source.text: Under their supervision the eggs hatched into worms, and the worms spun silk threads.

translation.text: 在两人的照料下，蚕卵孵化成蚕，蚕又吐出丝线。

source.text: Byzantium was in the silk business at last.

translation.text: 拜占庭终于进入丝绸行业。

source.text: The Byzantine church and state created imperial workshops, monopolising production and keeping the secret to themselves.

translation.text: 拜占庭的教会和国家设立了皇家作坊，垄断生产，并严守其中的秘密。

source.text: This allowed a silk industry to be established, undercutting the market for ordinary-grade Chinese silk.

translation.text: 丝绸业由此建立起来，挤占了普通等级中国丝绸的市场。

source.text: However, high quality silk textiles, woven in China especially for the Middle Eastern market, continued to achieve high prices in the West, and trade along the Silk Road continued as before.

translation.text: 不过，中国专为中东市场织造的优质丝绸，在西方仍能卖出高价，丝绸之路上的贸易也照旧继续。

source.text: By the sixth century the Persians, too, had mastered the art of silk weaving, developing their own rich patterns and techniques.

translation.text: 到6世纪，波斯人也掌握了丝绸织造技术，并发展出自己华丽的图案和工艺。

source.text: But it wasn’t until the 13th century that Italy began silk production, with the introduction of 2,000 skilled silk weavers from Constantinople.

translation.text: 但直到13世纪，随着2,000名来自君士坦丁堡的熟练丝织工到来，意大利才开始生产丝绸。

source.text: Eventually, silk production became widespread throughout Europe.

translation.text: 最终，丝绸生产遍及欧洲。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: World silk production has approximately doubled during the last 30 years in spite of manmade fibres replacing certain uses of silk. Before this period, China and Japan were the two main producers, together manufacturing more than 50 per cent of world production each year. After the late 1970s, however, China dramatically increased its silk production, and once again became the world’s leading producer.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 尽管人造纤维取代了丝绸的某些用途，过去30年间，世界丝绸产量仍大约翻了一番。在这之前，中国和日本是两大主要生产国，两国每年合计生产全球50%以上的丝绸。然而，20世纪70年代末以后，中国大幅提高丝绸产量，再次成为世界第一大生产国。

translation.text: 尽管人造纤维取代了丝绸的某些用途，过去30年间，世界丝绸产量仍大约翻了一番。

translation.text: 在这之前，中国和日本是两大主要生产国，两国每年合计生产全球50%以上的丝绸。

passages.title: The Early History of Olive Oil

headerUnits.sourceNormalizedText: The Early History of Olive Oil

source.text: The Early History of Olive Oil

translation.text: 橄榄油的早期历史

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Olive oil is produced from the fruit of the olive tree, which is a member of the Oleaceae plant family. The trees require some cold weather during the year, but also tolerate hot, dry conditions, and do not like moisture when they are flowering. They actually produce better when subjected to these stressful conditions, and as a result, olive trees have traditionally been grown on land where little else will survive.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 橄榄油由橄榄树的果实制成，橄榄树属于木犀科植物。橄榄树一年中需要经历一段寒冷天气，但也能忍受炎热、干燥的环境，而且在开花时不喜欢潮湿。实际上，承受这些不利条件反而会让它们结出更多果实。因此，传统上人们常在几乎没有其他植物能够存活的土地上种植橄榄树。

source.text: They actually produce better when subjected to these stressful conditions, and as a result, olive trees have traditionally been grown on land where little else will survive.

translation.text: 实际上，承受这些不利条件反而会让它们结出更多果实。因此，传统上人们常在几乎没有其他植物能够存活的土地上种植橄榄树。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Archaeologists today are divided over exactly where the first domestication of the olive occurred: some say it was in the area which is now Iran, Syria, Jordan and Egypt, while others contend it was in mainland Greece or on the island of Crete. The one thing that can be said with certainty is that cultivation began at least 6,000 years ago and spread slowly westward across the lands bordering on the Mediterranean Sea. Olive oil was used for a variety of purposes during these early times, including as a pharmacological ointment and in rituals for anointing royalty.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 如今，考古学家对于橄榄最早究竟在何处被驯化仍意见不一：有人认为是在今天的伊朗、叙利亚、约旦和埃及一带，另一些人则主张是在希腊大陆或克里特岛。有一点可以确定：橄榄种植至少始于6,000年前，随后沿地中海沿岸地区缓慢向西传播。在早期，橄榄油用途多样，包括制成药用软膏，以及用于为王室成员涂油的仪式。

translation.text: 在早期，橄榄油用途多样，包括制成药用软膏，以及用于为王室成员涂油的仪式。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The ancient Greeks believed the olive tree was a priceless gift from the goddess Athena and used its oil in sacred religious rituals. In fact, the Greek poet Homer called olive oil ‘liquid gold’, and during the 6th and 7th centuries BC, Greek law forbade the cutting down of olive trees and made it punishable by death. The ancient Middle Eastern ruler King David valued his groves of olive trees and his olive oil warehouses so much that he posted guards around the clock to protect them.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 古希腊人认为，橄榄树是女神雅典娜赐予的无价礼物，并在神圣的宗教仪式中使用橄榄油。事实上，希腊诗人荷马把橄榄油称为“液体黄金”。公元前6和7世纪，希腊法律禁止砍伐橄榄树，违者可被判处死刑。古代中东统治者大卫王极为珍视自己的橄榄园和橄榄油仓库，甚至安排守卫昼夜不停地保护它们。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Over the years, olive oil developed other uses. Its employment in cooking dates at least as far back as the 5th century BC, as described by the Greek philosopher Plato. Its use as an aid to beauty and health later became ingrained in many Mediterranean cultures. The Romans, for example, are said to have used generous amounts on their bodies to moisturise their skin after bathing. With the spread of the Roman Empire, olive oil became a major commodity, and its trade promoted commerce throughout the ancient world. It is generally believed that in the 1st–2nd centuries BC, olive trees were taken to North Africa and then to Spain, which was later to become the world’s largest producer of olive oil. Artefacts found at various Mediterranean archaeological sites include olive oil storage vessels with olive plant residue still in them. Historical evidence still in existence in the form of wall paintings and ancient manuscripts (including the works of the Roman naturalist and philosopher, Pliny the Elder) all record production techniques and the various uses of olive oil.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 随着岁月推移，橄榄油又有了其他用途。希腊哲学家柏拉图的记述表明，人们至少早在公元前5世纪就已用橄榄油烹饪。后来，用橄榄油美容和保健的习惯深深融入许多地中海文化。例如，据说罗马人沐浴后会在身上大量涂抹橄榄油，为皮肤保湿。随着罗马帝国扩张，橄榄油成为重要商品，它的贸易推动了整个古代世界的商业发展。人们普遍认为，公元前1至2世纪，橄榄树被带到北非，随后又传入西班牙；西班牙后来成为世界最大的橄榄油生产国。地中海各处考古遗址发现的文物中，包括一些仍留有橄榄植物残渣的储油容器。以壁画和古代手稿形式保存至今的历史证据——其中包括罗马博物学家兼哲学家老普林尼（Pliny the Elder）的著作——都记录了橄榄油的生产技术和各种用途。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Making olive oil in those early days was a laborious process accomplished without mechanisation. Processing or milling the fruit involved several distinct stages to extract the liquid. The olives were harvested from the trees by hand or by beating the fruit from the trees with long sticks. The olives were then rinsed and crushed to separate out the large seed found in the centre of each. The remaining seedless flesh was put in woven bags and pressed. Hot water was then poured over the bags to separate the oil from the solid bits of olive. The liquid produced in this process, consisting of oil and water, was drained into stone basins or tanks, where it was allowed to settle and separate. In cold weather, a bit of salt was added to speed up the process. As much oil as possible was drawn off the water, but the result was still not pure oil. Therefore, this impure mixture was allowed once more to settle in vats and then separated in order to refine the product.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 早期制作橄榄油没有机械辅助，是一项十分费力的工作。加工或碾磨果实需要经过几个不同阶段，才能提取液体。人们用手采摘橄榄，或用长棍敲打，让果实从树上落下。橄榄随后被冲洗、压碎，以分离出每颗果实中央的大果核。剩下的无核果肉装入编织袋中压榨。接着，人们把热水浇在袋子上，使油与橄榄的固体碎屑分离。由油和水组成的液体被排入石盆或石槽中，静置后自行分层。天气寒冷时，还会加入少量盐来加快这一过程。人们尽可能从水面撇取油，但得到的仍不是纯油。因此，这种含有杂质的混合物要再次放入大桶中静置并分离，以进一步提纯。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The waste water from the milling process, which is called amurca, is a bitter-tasting and foul-smelling liquid. In many ancient civilisations it was often simply discarded, causing serious pollution because of its acidity and high salt content. However, in the Roman period it was regarded as a very useful substance. When spread on surfaces, amurca forms a hard finish and therefore it was often applied to the floors of grain storage buildings where it hardened, keeping out water, mud and pests. When boiled down, amurca was applied to leather to soften it so that it was easier to shape into articles of clothing and shoes. It could also be eaten by farm animals and was, in fact, fed to livestock suffering from malnutrition. According to ancient texts, amurca was also utilised in moderate amounts by farmers as a fertiliser or as a pesticide, helping them to protect their crops from insects and even small rodents.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 碾磨过程产生的废水称为 amurca，是一种味苦、气味难闻的液体。在许多古代文明中，人们常常直接把它倒掉；由于它酸性强、含盐量高，会造成严重污染。然而在罗马时期，人们认为它非常有用。amurca 涂在物体表面会形成坚硬的表层，因此常被铺在粮仓地面上；硬化后，它可以阻挡水、泥和害虫。amurca 煮浓后还可涂在皮革上，使皮革变软，更容易制成衣物和鞋。农场动物也可以食用它；事实上，人们曾用它喂养营养不良的牲畜。据古代文献记载，农民还会适量使用 amurca 作为肥料或杀虫剂，以保护作物免受昆虫甚至小型啮齿动物侵害。

passages.title: The extinction of the cave bear

headerUnits.sourceNormalizedText: The extinction of the cave bear

source.text: The extinction of the cave bear

translation.text: 洞熊的灭绝

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Hervé Bocherens, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Tübingen, Germany, says his colleagues find his research methods a little ‘crude’. He dissolves 30,000-year-old animal bones in hydrochloric acid, which is strong enough to burn through metal, soaks the bone solution in lye, cooks it at about 200 degrees Fahrenheit and freeze-dries it, until what’s left is a speck of powder weighing less than one one-hundredth of an ounce. The method may be harsh, but the yield is precious – the biography of a cave bear as told through its chemical components. Bocherens is at the forefront of research on the bear, a European species that died out 25,000 years ago. People have been excavating cave bear remains for hundreds of years— in the Middle Ages, the massive skulls were attributed to dragons — but the past decade has seen a burst of discoveries about how the bears lived and why they became extinct. An abundance of bones has been found from Spain to Romania in caves where the animals once hibernated. ‘Caves are good places to preserve bones, and cave bears had the good sense to die there,’ Bocherens says.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 德国蒂宾根大学的进化生物学家 Hervé Bocherens 说，同事们觉得他的研究方法有点“粗暴”。他把3万年前的动物骨骼溶解在足以腐蚀金属的盐酸中，再用碱液浸泡骨骼溶液，以约200华氏度加热，最后进行冷冻干燥，直到只剩下一小点重量不到百分之一盎司的粉末。这种方法或许很严苛，但所得成果十分珍贵——骨骼的化学成分讲述了一只洞熊的一生。Bocherens 处在洞熊研究的前沿；这种欧洲物种在2.5万年前灭绝。数百年来，人们一直在发掘洞熊遗骸——中世纪时，那些巨大的头骨还被认为属于龙——但过去十年间，关于洞熊如何生活以及为何灭绝的新发现突然大量涌现。从西班牙到罗马尼亚，人们在这些动物曾经冬眠的洞穴里发现了大量骨骼。“洞穴很适合保存骨骼，而洞熊很明智，选择死在那里。”Bocherens 说。

source.text: Hervé Bocherens, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Tübingen, Germany, says his colleagues find his research methods a little ‘crude’.

translation.text: 德国蒂宾根大学的进化生物学家 Hervé Bocherens 说，同事们觉得他的研究方法有点“粗暴”。

source.text: He dissolves 30,000-year-old animal bones in hydrochloric acid, which is strong enough to burn through metal, soaks the bone solution in lye, cooks it at about 200 degrees Fahrenheit and freeze-dries it, until what’s left is a speck of powder weighing less than one one-hundredth of an ounce.

translation.text: 他把3万年前的动物骨骼溶解在足以腐蚀金属的盐酸中，再用碱液浸泡骨骼溶液，以约200华氏度加热，最后进行冷冻干燥，直到只剩下一小点重量不到百分之一盎司的粉末。

source.text: The method may be harsh, but the yield is precious – the biography of a cave bear as told through its chemical components.

translation.text: 这种方法或许很严苛，但所得成果十分珍贵——骨骼的化学成分讲述了一只洞熊的一生。

source.text: Bocherens is at the forefront of research on the bear, a European species that died out 25,000 years ago.

translation.text: Bocherens 处在洞熊研究的前沿；这种欧洲物种在2.5万年前灭绝。

source.text: People have been excavating cave bear remains for hundreds of years— in the Middle Ages, the massive skulls were attributed to dragons — but the past decade has seen a burst of discoveries about how the bears lived and why they became extinct.

translation.text: 数百年来，人们一直在发掘洞熊遗骸——中世纪时，那些巨大的头骨还被认为属于龙——但过去十年间，关于洞熊如何生活以及为何灭绝的新发现突然大量涌现。

source.text: An abundance of bones has been found from Spain to Romania in caves where the animals once hibernated.

translation.text: 从西班牙到罗马尼亚，人们在这些动物曾经冬眠的洞穴里发现了大量骨骼。

source.text: ‘Caves are good places to preserve bones, and cave bears had the good sense to die there,’ Bocherens says.

translation.text: “洞穴很适合保存骨骼，而洞熊很明智，选择死在那里。”Bocherens 说。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Along with mammoths, lions and woolly rhinos, cave bears (Ursus spelaeus) were once among Europe’s most impressive creatures. Males weighed up to 1,500 pounds, 50 per cent more than the largest modern grizzly bears. Cave bears had wider heads than today’s bears, and powerful shoulders and forelimbs. But the relationship between humans and cave bears has been mysterious. Were humans prey for the bears, or predators? Were bears the object of worship or fear?
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 洞熊（Ursus spelaeus）曾与猛犸象、狮子和披毛犀一道，成为欧洲最引人注目的动物之一。雄性洞熊体重最高可达1,500磅，比现今体型最大的灰熊还重50%。洞熊的头部比今天的熊更宽，肩部和前肢也十分强壮。然而，人类与洞熊之间的关系一直令人费解。人类是熊的猎物，还是熊的捕食者？熊受到的是崇拜，还是恐惧？

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Initially cave bears shared the continent of Europe, more than 100,000 years ago, with Neanderthals, a primitive species of humans. Modern humans arrived in Europe about 40,000 years ago, and were soon aware of the bears. They painted images of the animals on cave walls, and carved their likeness in fragments of mammoth tusk. The walls of France’s Chauvet cave are painted with lions, hyenas and bears; dating back 32,000 years, these are perhaps the oldest paintings in the world. The painters weren’t the cave’s only occupants: the floor is covered with 150 cave bear skeletons, and its soft clay still holds paw prints. Most dramatically, a cave bear skull was perched on a stone slab in the center of one chamber, placed deliberately by some long-gone cave inhabitant. ‘There’s no way to tell if it was just curiosity that made someone put a skull on the rock, or if it had religious significance,’ says Bocherens.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 10万多年前，洞熊最初与较原始的人类物种尼安德特人共同生活在欧洲大陆。现代人大约在4万年前到达欧洲，并很快注意到洞熊。他们在洞壁上画下洞熊的形象，还用猛犸象牙碎片雕刻出它们的样子。法国肖维洞穴的墙壁上画有狮子、鬣狗和熊；这些画可追溯到3.2万年前，或许是世界上最古老的绘画。作画者并不是洞穴唯一的居住者：洞穴地面布满150具洞熊骨架，松软的黏土中至今仍留有熊掌印。最引人注目的是，在一个洞室中央，一只洞熊头骨被放在石板上，显然是某位早已离去的洞穴居住者有意摆放的。“我们无法判断，那个人把头骨放到石头上只是出于好奇，还是这个举动具有宗教意义。”Bocherens 说。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Another discovery, hundreds of miles to the east of Chauvet, would shed light on the relationship between cave bears and humans. The Swabian Jura is a limestone plateau in southwestern Germany that is riddled with caves. A steel gate guards the Hohle Fels cave from vandals and curiosity-seekers. Floodlights in the cave’s main chamber illuminate the ceiling, vaulted like a cathedral above 5,000 square feet of floor space. Long ago, as shown by the bones and tools that archaeologists have found, cave bears and human beings sought shelter here from winter weather.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Cave bears disappeared not long after humans spread throughout Europe, and one theory is that hunting led to the bears’ extinction. Hervé Bocherens’ test tubes may hold the clues. Running his white powder through a mass spectrometer, he identifies different isotopes, or chemical forms, of elements such as carbon and nitrogen that reflect what the bears were eating and how quickly they grew. After studying hundreds of bones from dozens of sites in Europe, Bocherens has found that cave bears ate mainly plants.

passages.title: The history of the bar code

headerUnits.sourceNormalizedText: The history of the bar code

source.text: The history of the bar code

translation.text: 条形码的历史

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The first step toward today’s bar codes came in 1948, when Bernard Silver, a graduate student in the USA, overheard a conversation in the halls of Philadelphia’s Drexel Institute of Technology. The president of a food chain was pleading with a professor to undertake research on a method of capturing product information automatically at store checkouts. The professor turned down the request, but Bernard Silver mentioned the conversation to his friend Norman Woodland, a twenty-seven-year-old teacher at Drexel.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 通向现代条形码的第一步始于1948年。当时，美国研究生 Bernard Silver 在费城德雷塞尔理工学院的走廊里偶然听到一段谈话。一家连锁食品店的负责人正恳请一位教授研究一种方法，以便在商店结账时自动获取商品信息。教授拒绝了这个请求，但 Bernard Silver 把这段谈话告诉了朋友 Norman Woodland；后者27岁，是德雷塞尔的一名教师。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The problem fascinated the two friends, and they set about thinking of a solution. Their first idea was to use patterns printed with an ink that would glow under ultraviolet light, and they built a device to test the concept. It worked, but the printing costs were high and the patterns faded over time. Nonetheless, they were convinced they had a workable idea. After several months of work they came up with the linear bar code, using elements from two established technologies: Morse code, in which letters and numbers are coded into a system of dots and dashes, and the method used to record soundtracks in movies. Silver and Woodland patented the idea in 1952, describing their invention as ‘article classification… through the medium of identifying patterns’. But the cost, together with the fact that their scanning equipment was rather unreliable, made the idea a non-starter at that time.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Scanning systems made little progress until the 1970s, when lasers became affordable. Following this, various systems came into use around the world in stores, libraries, factories, and the like, each with its own proprietary code, but there was no standardization. A consortium of grocery manufacturers and retailers therefore set up a committee to look into bar codes, and to standardize what became known formally as the Universal Product Code (UPC). At the heart of the committee’s guidelines were a few basic principles. To make life easier for the cashier, bar codes would have to be readable from almost any angle and at a range of distances. Because they would be reproduced by the million, the labels would have to be cheap and easy to print. And to be affordable, automated checkout systems would have to pay for themselves in two and a half years.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The committee considered more than a dozen versions of bar codes, including one based on multi-colored dots and another using a circular bull’s-eye design with lines radiating from a central point. On April 1, 1973, they unanimously agreed on a standardized UPC, a combination of black and white lines and numbers, based on Woodland and Silver’s idea but developed by George Laurer at IBM. Alan Haberman, who headed the subcommittee as president of First National Stores, described the bar code as a kind of world language that worked for everyone. Each of the tens of thousands of grocery outlets in the US had to spend at least $200,000 on new scanning equipment. Chains had to install new data processing centers and retrain their employees. passages.title: The history of the British wool industry

headerUnits.sourceNormalizedText: The history of the British wool industry

source.text: The history of the British wool industry

translation.text: 英国羊毛业的历史

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Wool is part of Britain’s history and heritage, more so than any other commodity ever produced in that country. It was made into cloth there in the Bronze Age, which began about 1900 BC. By the time the Romans invaded in 55 BC the Britons had developed a wool industry, and this was encouraged by their new masters. Roman emperors appreciated the fineness of British woollen cloth. Although Saxon invasions in the fifth century nearly destroyed the industry, it is known that in the eighth century Britain was exporting woollen fabrics to continental Europe, and after the arrival of the Norman conquerors in 1066 the industry expanded. By the twelfth century, wool was becoming England’s greatest national asset. Cloth making was widespread, particularly in the large towns of southern and eastern England, nearest to France. But the greatest wealth came from exports of raw wool.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 在英国生产过的各种商品中，羊毛与这个国家的历史和传统联系最为紧密。大约始于公元前1900年的青铜时代，英国人就已用羊毛织布。到罗马人于公元前55年入侵时，不列颠人已经发展出羊毛产业，新统治者又推动了这个行业。罗马皇帝十分欣赏英国毛织品的细腻。尽管5世纪撒克逊人的入侵几乎摧毁了这一产业，但可以确定的是，8世纪时英国已向欧洲大陆出口毛织品；1066年诺曼征服者到来后，该产业进一步扩张。到12世纪，羊毛逐渐成为英格兰最重要的国家资产。制布业分布广泛，在最靠近法国的英格兰南部和东部大城镇尤其兴盛。不过，最大的财富来自未经加工的羊毛出口。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Kings and their ministers welcomed the revenue that resulted from exports and export taxes – and also the power it gave to the king, who could grant or withdraw permits for the wool towns and for the industry. Trade associations, known as ‘guilds’, were founded to guarantee good work by experienced weavers (people who produce cloth from woollen threads), and were powerful for hundreds of years. The peak of cloth production was reached in the thirteenth century. Then the wool trade declined for a long period because of political conflict.

translation.text: 毛织品产量在13世纪达到顶峰，随后羊毛贸易因政治冲突而长期衰退。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: In 1331, King Edward III encouraged master weavers from Flanders (an area of present-day Belgium) to settle in England. These Flemish weavers and their descendants were to play a part in the final development of English cloth. The export trade in raw wool recovered and the first half of the fourteenth century was a time of prosperity for English wool farmers. But it was overshadowed by a long war with France (export taxes on wool were one of the principal means of financing the war) and by bubonic plague (the Black Death), which in 1349 caused devastation: in many villages as much as three-quarters of the population died. This led to an increase of the sheep flocks, for there were not enough people left to cultivate the land for arable crops.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Despite setbacks, raw wool exporting expanded, and so also did manufacturing of wool fabrics. This was becoming both specialised and localised. The area of England known as the West Country had three advantages – extensive sheep pastures, a supply of soft water for washing, scouring and dyeing wool, and water-power to drive machinery. Similarly, the hills of Yorkshire and Lancashire in the north of England had soft water and fast running streams. Water from the latter could be used to drive mills for ‘fulling’, a shrinking process which makes the fabric firmer and its surface more compact.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: In East Anglia there was soft water, but no hills or fast-running streams to provide power for fulling mills. Instead, East Anglia used the long, fine wool from its native sheep breeds to produce a cloth which did not require the fulling process. This was the type of cloth which is now called ‘worsted’, after the village of Worstead. For four hundred years East Anglia dominated the worsted trade, with skills inherited from the Flemish settlers of 1331.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: English cloth quickly achieved an international reputation. From being primarily a raw wool exporter, the country became in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries a manufacturer and exporter of cloth. At the end of the fifteenth century, it was said that England was largely a nation of sheep farmers and cloth manufacturers. The next two centuries saw continued expansion of the industry despite conflicts at home and abroad. In the sixteenth century, French weavers, persecuted for their Protestant religion, sought refuge in England and took their skills with them. England began to surpass Flanders in woollen manufacture; by the end of the seventeenth century it comprised two-thirds of the value of its exports. Radical changes lay ahead, in the geographical location of the industry, in labour use and in manufacturing processes. By 1770, output of worsted from Yorkshire equalled that of East Anglia, and its cloth manufacturing district began to take shape with the expansion of major towns: Leeds, Bradford, Halifax, Huddersfield, and Wakefield.

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The Industrial Revolution of 1750–1850 also brought change. It led the way for new inventions stemming from the Lancashire cotton industry, to mechanize and speed dramatically the processes of spinning and weaving. Manufacturing methods, unchanged since the revival of the trade in the fourteenth century, were now superseded. Mechanization had been opposed in the past and it was again. The widespread unrest of 1812 led to the destruction of equipment by bands of rioters, who feared they would lose employment. But machinery won the day.

source.text: The History of the Pencil

translation.text: 铅笔的历史

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: The history of the pencil starts with a violent thunderstorm. When some particularly ferocious weather struck the Lake District in North West England in the sixteenth century, locals in the village of Borrowdale discovered a large uprooted tree. Underneath the tree lay an unknown black substance which we now know as graphite. It was slightly shiny and smooth to the touch. And it left a black smear on the hands of all who touched it.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 铅笔的历史始于一场猛烈的雷暴。16世纪，英格兰西北部湖区遭遇一次格外凶猛的暴风雨，Borrowdale 村的居民发现了一棵被连根拔起的大树。树下有一种当时不为人知的黑色物质，也就是我们今天所说的石墨。它略带光泽，摸起来很光滑，任何人碰过以后，手上都会留下黑色痕迹。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Initially, the local farmers used the newly discovered material as a handy way to identify their sheep. However, others quickly realised the potential for using this intriguing substance to write on paper. When it was untreated the material was very soft, which meant that it was messy to handle. To make it fit for use with paper, people enclosed a thin core of the substance in stiff sheep hides or rope. At this time chemistry was still in its infancy. People searched for a word to describe this increasingly useful substance and came up with plumbago which, in Latin, means acts or writes like lead. Later the name was changed to graphite. But because words have remarkable staying power, we still call graphite the lead of a pencil even though it is now known that there is no trace of real lead in graphite.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 起初，当地农民把这种新发现的材料当作给自家绵羊做标记的方便工具。不过，其他人很快意识到，这种奇特物质还可以用来在纸上书写。未经处理时，这种材料很软，使用起来容易弄脏。为了让它适合写在纸上，人们用硬羊皮或绳子包住一根细细的材料芯。当时，化学仍处于起步阶段。人们寻找一个词来描述这种越来越有用的物质，最后称它为 plumbago；这个词在拉丁语中意为“性质或书写效果像铅”。后来，它被改名为石墨。但词语具有惊人的延续力，所以即使如今人们已经知道石墨中没有一丝真正的铅，我们仍把铅笔中的石墨芯称为“铅”。

blocks.sourceNormalizedText: Graphite has a very high melting point at around 3,500 degrees Celsius. This made it invaluable to the British army and navy as a secret ingredient in the manufacture of cannon balls. The Royal Ordnance, or weaponry section of the British armed forces, used graphite as a lining inside the moulds for cannon balls, which, as a result, the British could turn out faster and more cheaply than their European rivals. In addition to its value to the armed forces, the government quickly realised the commercial potential of the graphite at Borrowdale, and assumed control of all the mines there during the sixteenth century. Armed guards accompanied the precious graphite all the way down to the metal foundries by the naval shipyards in the south of England. The graphite was so valuable that the locals, who called it wad, started to steal it. As a deterrent, an act of Parliament in 1752 made this offence punishable by time in prison.
blocks.translationNormalizedText: 石墨的熔点非常高，约为3,500摄氏度，因此成为英国陆军和海军制造炮弹时极有价值的一种秘密材料。英国武装部队负责军械的皇家军械部门，用石墨为炮弹模具制作内衬；这样一来，英国生产炮弹的速度比欧洲对手更快，成本也更低。除了对军队的重要性，政府也很快意识到 Borrowdale 石墨的商业潜力，于16世纪接管了当地所有矿井。武装守卫一路护送珍贵的石墨，把它运往英格兰南部海军造船厂附近的金属铸造厂。石墨价值极高，当地人把它称为 wad，并开始偷取。为了震慑偷盗者，1752年议会通过法案，规定这一罪行可判处监禁。
